paragraphs.paraphrase: At sunrise Telemachus and his crew sail into Pylos, 'the city of Neleus', where the townspeople are gathered on the beach sacrificing black bulls to Poseidon: nine groups of five hundred men, with nine bulls per group. While the Pylians are eating the 'inner meats' and burning the thigh bones as an offering to Poseidon, the travellers take in their sails, anchor and go ashore.

barriers.my_reading: 'They' are Telemachus and his crew (with Athena); they are only named in the last sentence, and the opening 'But' assumes the previous Book.
barriers.note: Book opens mid-story.

barriers.my_reading: Here 'they' switches to the Pylians at the sacrifice, not the travellers of the first sentence.
barriers.note: The arrival is also told twice ('they reached Pylos' ... 'Telemachus and his crew arrived').

barriers.my_reading: Neleus is presumably a past king of Pylos; ¶10 and ¶31 later show he is Nestor's dead father.
The internal organs of the sacrificed bulls (heart, liver, kidneys and so on), eaten first.
barriers.note: Sacrifice term never explained; recurs ¶4, ¶34 and is paired with 'outer meats' in ¶7, ¶35.

barriers.quote: burning the thigh bones on the embers in Poseidon’s name
barriers.my_reading: The thigh bones are burned as the god's share of the sacrifice while the people eat the meat.
barriers.note: Why thigh bones is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena walks ahead and Telemachus follows. She tells him not to be shy: he came on this voyage to learn where his father is buried and how he died, so he should go straight up to Nestor and ask him, since Nestor is a good man and will tell the truth.

barriers.my_reading: 'After a little while' / 'then' (older sense), not 'at present'.
barriers.note: Archaic sense; recurs ¶23, ¶36.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus, addressing his companion as 'Mentor', asks how he can dare approach Nestor and how he should address him, since he has no practice at long conversations and is embarrassed to question a man so much older than himself.

barriers.my_reading: Telemachus is speaking to Athena but believes she is Mentor, an older companion; she must be disguised as this man.
barriers.note: The disguise is never stated in this Book: the narrator says 'Athena' (¶1), Telemachus says 'Mentor', Pisistratus says 'sir' (¶5); only the eagle exit in ¶29 settles it. Heard aloud, 'Mentor' can sound like the ordinary noun 'mentor'. Outside knowledge confirms the disguise.

barriers.quote: dare I go up to Nestor
barriers.my_reading: 'How can I bring myself to approach Nestor?' - not the indignant modern 'how dare I'.
barriers.note: Inverted, old-fashioned word order.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena reassures him that some of what to say will come to him by instinct and the gods will prompt him with the rest, because she is sure the gods have been on his side since the day he was born.

They reach the gathered Pylians and find Nestor sitting with his sons while his men skewer and roast meat for the feast. The Pylians crowd round to welcome the strangers; Nestor's son Pisistratus seats them on sheepskins on the sand beside Nestor and his brother Thrasymedes, gives them portions of the 'inner meats', and pours wine into a gold cup, offering it to Athena first with a greeting.

barriers.my_reading: Preparing the main feast; since they arrived at sunrise, 'dinner' must mean the main meal of the day rather than an evening meal.
barriers.note: Time of day becomes confusing: sunrise arrival (¶0), 'dinner', then sunset in ¶25.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Pisistratus tells the older guest (Athena, whom he addresses as 'sir') to pray to Poseidon, because this is Poseidon's feast, make a drink offering, and then pass the cup to his friend to do the same. He is sure the younger man prays too, since no one can live without the gods, but because the younger man is about Pisistratus's own age he gives the elder the honour of going first.

barriers.my_reading: Pisistratus sees Athena as an older man (Mentor), so he calls her 'sir' while the narrator calls her 'her'.
barriers.note: Only makes sense if the reader has grasped the Mentor disguise (see ¶2).

barriers.my_reading: Poured out a little wine from the cup as a gift to the god before drinking.
barriers.note: The physical action is never shown anywhere in the Book; a reader may picture drinking a toast. Recurs ¶25, ¶26, ¶30.

barriers.quote: man cannot live without God in the world
barriers.my_reading: Everyone needs the gods; the singular capitalised 'God' in a world of many gods sounds Christian and jars.

barriers.quote: much of an age with myself
barriers.my_reading: About the same age as me.
barriers.note: Archaic idiom.

barriers.quote: I will give you the precedence
barriers.my_reading: I will let you go first, as the older man.
barriers.note: Old-fashioned phrasing.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena, pleased that Pisistratus served her first, prays to Poseidon: first bless Nestor and his sons, then reward the rest of the Pylians for their fine sacrifice, and finally give her and Telemachus success in the business that brought them to Pylos.

barriers.my_reading: Poseidon, as god of the sea, is pictured as the sea that surrounds the land.
barriers.note: The Book only calls Poseidon 'lord of the Earthquake'; the sea-god link relies on general knowledge.

barriers.quote: she began praying heartily to Poseidon
barriers.my_reading: Athena keeps up her disguise and prays like a mortal; a goddess praying to another god is puzzling unless the reader holds on to the disguise.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus prays in the same way after her. When the 'outer meats' have been roasted and taken off the skewers, carvers serve everyone and they all eat well; afterwards Nestor, 'the horseman of Gerene', begins to speak.

barriers.my_reading: After a while.
barriers.note: Archaic.

barriers.my_reading: The ordinary flesh of the bulls, roasted after the organs ('inner meats') were eaten.
barriers.note: The inner/outer pairing is never explained; recurs ¶35.

barriers.my_reading: Ate an excellent dinner (not cooked one).
barriers.note: Old idiom.

barriers.my_reading: A title for Nestor: Gerene is probably a place linked to him, and 'horseman' suggests he is famous for horses or chariots.
barriers.note: Never explained; low stakes because it clearly refers to Nestor.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nestor says that now the guests have eaten, it is the right time to ask who they are. He asks where they have sailed from and whether they are traders, or pirates who prey on everyone and are everyone's enemy.

barriers.quote: with your hand against every man and every man’s hand against you
barriers.my_reading: Living as outlaws or pirates who attack everyone and are attacked by everyone.
barriers.note: Biblical-sounding idiom.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus answers confidently, because Athena has given him the courage to ask about his father and so earn himself a good reputation.

Telemachus greets Nestor respectfully and says they come from Ithaca on private, not public, business: he wants news of his father Odysseus, who fought beside Nestor at Troy. The fates of the other heroes are known, but no one can say whether or where Odysseus died, on land or at sea. He begs Nestor, as a suppliant, to tell him plainly whatever he saw or heard of Odysseus's death, without softening it out of pity, and to repay any help Odysseus once gave him at Troy by telling the whole truth.

barriers.my_reading: The Achaeans are the Greeks who fought at Troy, Nestor's side; this is only implied by 'you Achaeans ... among the Trojans' later in the speech.
barriers.note: Never explained; 'Argives' is later used for the same army.

barriers.my_reading: Ithaca, Telemachus's home island, lying below a mountain called Neritum.
barriers.note: 'Under' suggests a mountain, but nothing says what Neritum is.

barriers.my_reading: A poetic name for the sea, probably after a sea goddess.
barriers.note: Sea goddess: outside knowledge only.

barriers.quote: I come as a suppliant to your knees
barriers.my_reading: I come humbly begging you, as if kneeling and clasping your knees.
barriers.note: 'Suppliant' is uncommon; the knee-clasping gesture is outside knowledge only; 'to your knees' is odd English.

barriers.my_reading: Being hard-pressed and harassed while fighting in the Trojans' land.
Tell me the whole truth.
barriers.note: Archaic word order; sounds odd aloud.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nestor says the question brings back a time of great suffering, at sea on raids under Achilles and in the fighting at Troy, where the best men died - Ajax, Achilles, Patroclus and Nestor's own son Antilochus - and the full story could not be told in five or six years. For nine years they tried every trick while the gods were against them, and no one matched Odysseus for cunning. Nestor marvels that Telemachus looks and talks just like his father, and says he and Odysseus always agreed and advised the army together.

barriers.my_reading: Troy; Priam is presumably its king.
barriers.note: The link is only made by 'the city of Priam' (¶12) matching 'the town of Troy' (¶10).

barriers.quote: compare with your father in subtlety
barriers.my_reading: Cunning, craftiness, skill at tricks.
barriers.note: 'Subtlety' in an older sense.

barriers.quote: if indeed you are his son. I can hardly believe my eyes
barriers.my_reading: Nestor is amazed at how much Telemachus resembles Odysseus in looks and speech; the 'if' expresses amazement rather than real doubt.
barriers.note: The physical resemblance is only implied.

barriers.my_reading: Never disagreed.
The Argives seem to be the whole Greek army - another name for the Achaeans.
barriers.note: Never explained; later 'Argos' names particular places (¶14, ¶20, ¶21), which suggests Argives might be only people from Argos.

paragraphs.paraphrase: After they sacked Troy and set sail, scattered by the gods, Zeus made the Greeks' voyage home hard, because not all of them had behaved wisely or rightly. Many came to a bad end through the anger of Athena, Zeus's daughter, who caused a quarrel between the two sons of Atreus.

barriers.my_reading: Probably 'and the gods scattered our fleet'; the timing is unclear because they are only just setting sail.

barriers.quote: they had not all been either wise or understanding
barriers.my_reading: Some Greeks had behaved foolishly or wrongly (perhaps an offence against the gods), which angered Athena; the offence is never specified.
barriers.note: What they did: outside knowledge only.

barriers.my_reading: The brothers Agamemnon and Menelaus, as ¶13 shows.
barriers.note: Only inferable from the next paragraph.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Agamemnon and Menelaus called an assembly the wrong way, at sunset when the troops were drunk. Menelaus wanted to sail home at once; Agamemnon wanted to stay and make great sacrifices to calm Athena's anger - foolishly, says Nestor, because the gods do not change their minds easily. The brothers exchanged harsh words and the army jumped up shouting, divided over what to do.

barriers.quote: he would not prevail with her
barriers.my_reading: Agamemnon would not win Athena over with sacrifices.
barriers.note: 'Prevail with' is old-fashioned.

barriers.my_reading: The army split into two opposing camps (not each man individually undecided).
barriers.note: The modern idiom means personal indecision; ¶14 shows a literal split in half.

paragraphs.paraphrase: After a night of resentment, half the army (Nestor's half) launched their ships with their goods and women while the other half stayed with Agamemnon. At Tenedos a second quarrel sent some ships back to Agamemnon under Odysseus, but Nestor pushed on with the son of Tydeus (Diomed); Menelaus caught up at Lesbos, a sign from the gods sent them straight across the open sea to Euboea, and a good wind took them overnight to Geraestus, where they sacrificed to Poseidon. Four days later Diomed's men put in at Argos, and Nestor sailed on to Pylos with a steady fair wind.

barriers.my_reading: Probably women captured at Troy as war prizes rather than wives.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only; a reader may picture wives travelling with the army.

barriers.my_reading: Diomed, who is named later in the same paragraph going home to Argos.
barriers.note: Two names for one person, never explicitly linked.

barriers.quote: whether to go outside Chios by the island of Psyra, keeping this to our left, or inside Chios, over against the stormy headland of Mimas
barriers.my_reading: A choice of route: round the seaward side of the island of Chios past Psyra, or through the channel between Chios and the mainland, opposite the dangerous cape of Mimas.
barriers.note: Cannot be pictured without a map; 'this' (Psyra or Chios?) is ambiguous; 'over against' is archaic.

barriers.my_reading: Diomed's men brought their ships home to Argos, Diomed's home.
barriers.note: 'Stationed' is odd; 'Argos' is later used for Agamemnon's realm (¶20, ¶21) while 'Argives' means all the Greeks.

barriers.my_reading: The wind never died down.
barriers.note: Nautical/old phrasing.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nestor says he reached home without news of the others and can only pass on reports: the Myrmidons came home under Achilles's son Neoptolemus, Philoctetes (son of Poias) got back safely, and Idomeneus brought all his surviving men home to Crete. Everyone has heard that Aegisthus killed Agamemnon and was soon killed in turn by Agamemnon's son Orestes, which shows how good it is to leave a son behind. He urges Telemachus, a tall, fine-looking young man, to prove his courage and win fame too.

barriers.my_reading: The people or troops who had followed Achilles, now led home by his son.
Treacherous Aegisthus.
barriers.note: Archaic epithet; recurs ¶20, ¶23.

barriers.my_reading: Handsome, fine-looking (an American reader may take 'smart-looking' as 'clever-looking').

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus agrees that the Greeks praise Orestes, whose fame will last forever for avenging his father. He wishes the gods would let him take similar revenge on the arrogant suitors who mistreat him and plot his ruin, but says the gods have no such luck in store for him or his father, so they must put up with it.

barriers.my_reading: Men courting Telemachus's mother, as Nestor explains in ¶17.
barriers.note: Assumes earlier Books; explained only in the next paragraph.

barriers.quote: grant me to take such vengeance
barriers.my_reading: Allow me to take such revenge.
barriers.note: Archaic construction.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nestor remembers hearing that Telemachus's mother has many suitors who are hostile to him and are wasting his property, and asks whether he is putting up with it meekly or whether the people and some sign from the gods are against him. Perhaps Odysseus will return and punish them, alone or with an army; and if Athena favoured Telemachus as openly as she favoured Odysseus at Troy, the suitors would soon lose interest in courting.

barriers.my_reading: Ruining and wasting his property and household.

barriers.quote: are public feeling and the voice of heaven against you?
barriers.my_reading: Is he held back because the people of Ithaca and some divine message (an oracle?) favour the suitors?
barriers.note: 'The voice of heaven' is not explained.

barriers.quote: Who knows but that Odysseus may come back
barriers.my_reading: Perhaps Odysseus will still come back.
barriers.note: Archaic construction; can be parsed as 'Who knows? But ...'.

barriers.quote: some of these wooers would soon forget their wooing
barriers.my_reading: The suitors ('wooers') would soon stop courting - an understatement for being driven off or killed.
barriers.note: 'Wooers' is a second name for the suitors.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus says he can expect nothing like that; it is far too much to hope for and he dares not even think about it, and even if the gods wanted it, such good fortune could never come to him.

barriers.quote: Even if the gods themselves willed it, no such good fortune could come to me.
barriers.my_reading: A despairing exaggeration: he feels so hopeless he claims even the gods could not help - which Athena immediately rebukes.
barriers.note: Logic seems self-contradictory at first.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena (as Mentor) scolds him: the gods can reach far to save a man if they wish. She would rather suffer a long journey home and be safe on arrival than get home quickly and be murdered in her own house like Agamemnon, through the treachery of Aegisthus and 'his wife'; still, death comes to everyone, and when a man's time is up not even the gods who love him can save him.

barriers.quote: Heaven has a long arm if it is minded to save a man
barriers.my_reading: The gods can reach far and rescue someone if they choose to.
barriers.note: 'Is minded to' is old-fashioned.

barriers.quote: if it were me, I should not care how much I suffered before getting home
barriers.my_reading: Implicitly about Odysseus: a long hard return is better than a quick one that ends in murder, so his long absence is not hopeless.
barriers.note: The link to Odysseus is never stated.

barriers.my_reading: Agamemnon's wife (named in ¶21 as Clytemnestra), who conspired with Aegisthus - not a wife of Aegisthus.
barriers.note: 'His' most naturally attaches to Aegisthus; corrected only two paragraphs later.

barriers.my_reading: A qualification: the gods can rescue a man from danger but not from his fated death - perhaps hinting that Odysseus may be dead after all.
barriers.note: Seems to contradict 'Heaven has a long arm'; the point of the remark is unclear.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus asks Mentor to drop the subject: his father will never come back, the gods doomed him long ago. He turns to Nestor, who is said to have ruled through three generations and so seems almost immortal, and asks how Agamemnon was killed - where was Menelaus, and was it because Menelaus was away from Argos that the lesser man Aegisthus dared to murder him?

barriers.my_reading: Menelaus is Agamemnon's brother and would be expected to protect or avenge him.
barriers.note: The brotherhood is only implied by 'the two sons of Atreus' (¶12-13).

barriers.my_reading: The home region or kingdom of Agamemnon and Menelaus.
barriers.note: In ¶14 Argos was Diomed's home; in ¶23 Aegisthus rules 'in Mycenae' but feasts 'the people of Argos'; 'Argives' means all Greeks.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nestor says Telemachus has guessed right. If Menelaus had come home from Troy and found Aegisthus still alive, Aegisthus would have been killed and denied a grave, his body thrown outside the city for dogs and vultures, unmourned, because of his wicked crime. But while the Greeks were fighting at Troy, Aegisthus, lounging at home in Argos, kept flattering Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra.

barriers.quote: had found Aegisthus still alive in his house
barriers.my_reading: Menelaus arrived too late - Orestes had already killed Aegisthus (¶15, ¶23); 'his house' probably means Agamemnon's house that Aegisthus had taken over, or Aegisthus's own.
barriers.note: The counterfactual depends on a timeline explained only later.

barriers.quote: there would have been no mound heaped up for him, not even when he was dead
barriers.my_reading: He would have been killed and given no burial mound (grave).
barriers.note: Burial-mound custom unexplained; 'not even when he was dead' is awkward; the next clause clarifies.

paragraphs.paraphrase: At first Clytemnestra refused, being good by nature, and a bard whom Agamemnon had ordered to guard her was with her. But when the gods had doomed her, Aegisthus took the bard to a deserted island and left him to die and be eaten by birds, after which she willingly went to Aegisthus's house; he then thanked the gods with many sacrifices and rich gifts to temples, having succeeded beyond his hopes.

barriers.quote: there was a bard with her
barriers.my_reading: A court singer or poet whom Agamemnon had appointed to watch over his wife.
barriers.note: Why a singer would act as a guardian is unexplained.

barriers.quote: when heaven had decreed her destruction
barriers.my_reading: When the gods had fated her ruin - her fall into adultery and eventual death.
barriers.note: Blames the gods for her choice; 'heaven' again stands for the gods.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Meanwhile Nestor and Menelaus sailed home together; at Sunium near Athens, Apollo struck down Menelaus's expert helmsman Phrontis, and Menelaus stopped to bury him. Sailing on, Menelaus met a storm off Malea: part of his fleet was wrecked on the Cretan coast (the crews survived), while five ships were carried to Egypt, where he gathered great wealth among foreigners. Meanwhile Aegisthus killed Agamemnon and ruled Mycenae for seven years until, in the eighth, Orestes came back from Athens and killed him, then held a funeral feast for his mother and Aegisthus - on the very day Menelaus came home loaded with treasure.

barriers.quote: Sunium, which is the point of Athens
barriers.my_reading: A cape at the tip of the land around Athens.
barriers.note: 'Point' = cape/headland.

barriers.my_reading: Phrontis died suddenly and quietly at the helm, a death credited to Apollo's gentle arrows.
barriers.note: Sudden death as Apollo's arrows: outside knowledge only; a reader may think an arrow literally hit him, and 'painless' is puzzling.

barriers.quote: when he too could put to sea again
barriers.my_reading: 'Too' implies Nestor had already sailed on without waiting, which is not stated.
The headlands or cape of Malea.
barriers.note: 'Heads' = headlands.

barriers.quote: Here he divided his fleet and took the one half toward Crete
barriers.my_reading: The storm split Menelaus's fleet: part was wrecked on Crete, and Menelaus himself with five ships was carried to Egypt.
barriers.note: The text says he took half to Crete, then places him in Egypt with 'the other five ships'; contradictory on first pass and had to reread.

barriers.quote: for a small headland can make a great shelter
barriers.my_reading: Nestor is explaining where on the Cretan coast the ships were wrecked: the stretch near Gortyn and Phaestus is exposed to a south wind, the part beyond is sheltered by a small headland.
barriers.note: Hard to picture; the proverb-like aside and which 'Here' the wreck happened at are unclear.

barriers.my_reading: Wealth and possessions.
barriers.note: Archaic sense of 'substance'.

barriers.my_reading: Foreigners who spoke another language.
barriers.note: Archaic phrasing; 'alien' sounds odd aloud.

barriers.my_reading: 'Here at home' means back in Greece (Mycenae/Argos), not Pylos where Nestor is speaking.
Mycenae is Agamemnon's city, apparently within 'Argos'.
barriers.note: First mention of Mycenae; how it relates to 'Argos' and 'the people of Argos' is unclear.

barriers.quote: the funeral rites of his mother
barriers.my_reading: Orestes's mother Clytemnestra is suddenly dead; the text never says how (outside knowledge: Orestes killed her too).
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only; a reader will wonder how and why she died.

barriers.my_reading: Held the funeral, with a funeral feast; 'celebrated' sounds festive, and it is odd that he holds a funeral for the man he killed.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nestor advises Telemachus not to stay away from home long while such dangerous men are in his house, or they will eat up all his property and his journey will have been wasted. Still, he should visit Menelaus, just back from lands so remote that even birds could not cross the seas in a year; he can go by sea with his own crew, or by land with a chariot, horses and Nestor's sons as escorts to Lacedaemon, and Menelaus, an honest man, will tell him the truth.

barriers.quote: they will eat up everything you have among them
barriers.my_reading: Between them the suitors will consume all his property (they are literally feasting on his food).
barriers.note: 'Among them' = between them; the literal feasting is assumed from earlier Books.

barriers.quote: so far out of his reckoning
barriers.my_reading: So far off course.
barriers.note: Navigation idiom.

paragraphs.paraphrase: At sunset Athena (as Mentor) tells Nestor he has spoken well, but now they should have the sacrificed animals' tongues cut, mix wine for offerings to Poseidon and the other gods, and go to bed, since it is not right to stay late at a religious festival.

barriers.quote: have the tongues of the victims cut
barriers.my_reading: Cut out the tongues of the sacrificed bulls to burn them as a final offering.
barriers.note: 'Victims' = sacrificial animals (could first suggest people); the purpose of the tongues is unexplained.

barriers.my_reading: Dilute wine with water in a bowl, as ¶26 shows.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Everyone does as Athena says: servants wash the guests' hands, attendants fill the bowls with wine and water and serve it, the tongues are thrown on the fire, and everyone stands to make drink offerings. After drinking, Athena and Telemachus start to go back to their ship to sleep, but Nestor quickly stops them.

barriers.my_reading: Young male servants filled the bowls.
barriers.note: Sounds odd aloud (book pages).

barriers.quote: handed it round, after giving every man his drink offering
barriers.my_reading: The attendants first poured a little wine into each man's cup for the offering, then served the rest.
barriers.note: Order of actions is confusing; 'giving' the men their offering sounds backwards.

barriers.quote: were for going on board their ship
barriers.my_reading: Wanted to go back to the ship (to sleep).
barriers.note: Old-fashioned 'were for'.

barriers.my_reading: Nestor quickly intercepted them (caught up with them), or interrupted them.
barriers.note: British idiom.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nestor protests that the gods forbid they should leave him to sleep on a ship, as if he were too poor to have enough rugs and cloaks for himself and his guests. He has plenty, and neither he nor his sons after him will let Odysseus's son sleep on a ship's deck; they will always keep a hospitable house.

barriers.quote: that you should leave my house
barriers.my_reading: Leave his hospitality; they are still at the beach feast, not yet in his house.

barriers.quote: so poor and short of clothes, or that I have so few cloaks
barriers.my_reading: Cloaks and rugs double as bedding, so having plenty of them means he can give guests beds.
barriers.note: The clothes-bedding link is not explained.

barriers.my_reading: Welcome guests freely at any time.
barriers.note: Old idiom.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena (as Mentor) agrees that Telemachus should sleep at Nestor's house, but says she must go back to the ship to direct and encourage the crew, since she is the only older person among these young friends of Telemachus. Tomorrow she must go to the Cauconians to collect an old debt; she asks Nestor to send Telemachus on to Lacedaemon by chariot with one of his sons and his fastest horses.

barriers.quote: I must go to the Cauconians, where a large sum of money has long been owing to me
barriers.my_reading: A cover story to explain Mentor's departure; the Cauconians are some other people.
barriers.note: The text does not flag it as an excuse; a reader might take it at face value.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena then turns into an eagle and flies away, amazing everyone. Nestor takes Telemachus's hand and says he will be a great hero, since the gods escort him so young; the visitor was Athena herself, who favoured Odysseus at Troy. Nestor prays to her to bless him, his wife and children, and promises to sacrifice a one-year-old heifer that has never been worked, with gilded horns.

barriers.quote: none other of those who live in heaven than Zeus’s formidable daughter
barriers.my_reading: Of all the gods, it was none other than Athena.
barriers.note: Tangled word order.

barriers.my_reading: A title for Athena.
barriers.note: Who is meant is clear from context; what 'Trito' means is not (outside knowledge only).

barriers.quote: a yearling, unbroken, and never yet brought under the yoke
barriers.my_reading: A one-year-old young cow, not yet trained, never harnessed for work.
barriers.note: Farm vocabulary; 'unbroken' could be read as 'uninjured'.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena hears his prayer. Nestor leads his sons and sons-in-law to his house, mixes a bowl of sweet eleven-year-old wine that the housekeeper has just opened, and prays and pours offerings to Athena; after drinking, the others go to their own homes to sleep. Nestor puts Telemachus in the room above the gateway with Pisistratus, his only unmarried son still at home, and sleeps in an inner room beside his wife, the queen.

barriers.my_reading: Zeus who carries the aegis - some kind of magical shield or protective emblem.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only.

paragraphs.paraphrase: At dawn Nestor sits on the polished white marble benches in front of his house, where his late father Neleus used to sit, holding his scepter as protector of the community. His six sons - Echephron, Stratius, Perseus, Aretus, Thrasymedes and Pisistratus - gather round and give Telemachus a seat with them, and Nestor addresses them.

barriers.quote: Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning
barriers.my_reading: Sunrise personified as a goddess whose pink 'fingers' of light spread across the sky.
barriers.note: 'Child of morning' is puzzling since Dawn is the morning; recurs ¶36.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Nestor orders his sons to arrange a sacrifice to Athena, who appeared to them yesterday: one is to have the herdsman pick out a heifer and bring it from the plain, another to invite Telemachus's crew (leaving two men to guard the ship), another to fetch the goldsmith Laerceus to gild the heifer's horns. The rest are to have the maids prepare a fine meal and bring seats, firewood for the burnt offering, and clear spring water.

barriers.quote: tell the stockman to look me out a heifer
barriers.my_reading: Tell the cattle herder to pick out a young cow for me.
barriers.note: 'Stockman' and 'look me out' are British/old usage.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The sons carry out their tasks: the heifer, the crew and the goldsmith with his tools arrive, Athena herself comes to receive the sacrifice, and the smith gilds the horns with Nestor's gold to please her. Stratius and Echephron lead the heifer in by the horns, Aretus brings water in a patterned jug and a basket of barley meal, Thrasymedes stands ready with an axe and Perseus holds a bucket. Nestor washes his hands, sprinkles the barley and prays to Athena, throwing a tuft of the heifer's hair on the fire.

barriers.my_reading: Their separate, assigned errands.
barriers.note: Older sense of 'several'.

barriers.quote: Athena herself came to accept the sacrifice
barriers.my_reading: The goddess was present, probably unseen, to receive the offering.
barriers.note: Unclear whether anyone sees her.

barriers.my_reading: A jug or pitcher.
barriers.note: Uncommon word; aloud it sounds like 'ewe' or 'you're'.

barriers.my_reading: Presumably to catch the blood.
barriers.note: Purpose not stated.

barriers.my_reading: Scattering ground barley as part of the ritual.
barriers.note: Purpose unexplained.

barriers.quote: a lock from the heifer’s head
barriers.my_reading: A tuft of the heifer's hair.
barriers.note: 'Lock' without 'of hair'.

paragraphs.paraphrase: After the prayers, Thrasymedes fells the heifer with an axe blow that cuts the tendons of her neck, and Nestor's daughters, daughters-in-law and his elderly wife Eurydice cry out 'with delight'. They lift her head, Pisistratus cuts her throat, and when she has bled to death they butcher her; the thigh bones are wrapped in a double layer of fat topped with raw meat, and Nestor burns them and pours wine over them while young men hold five-pronged forks. Once the thighs are burnt and the 'inner meats' tasted, they cut up the rest of the meat and roast it on skewers.

barriers.my_reading: The women raise a loud cry at the moment of the kill; the text calls it delight, which reads as glee at the slaughter - perhaps a ritual cry.
barriers.note: Ritual cry: outside knowledge only; jarring for a modern reader.

barriers.my_reading: Five-tined roasting forks.
barriers.note: Hard to picture; a spit is usually a single rod.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Meanwhile Nestor's youngest daughter Polycaste bathes Telemachus, rubs him with oil and dresses him in a fine cloak and shirt; he comes out looking like a god and sits by Nestor. They eat the roasted meat, served wine in gold cups, and afterwards Nestor tells his sons to harness horses to a chariot for Telemachus so he can leave at once.

barriers.my_reading: Bathing a guest is a hospitality duty performed by the host's daughter.
barriers.note: Custom unexplained; may read as intimate or odd.

barriers.quote: put Telemachus’s horses to the chariot
barriers.my_reading: Harness the horses Nestor is lending him to the chariot.
barriers.note: Telemachus came by ship and has no horses of his own; 'put to' = harness.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The sons harness the fast horses, and the housekeeper packs bread, wine and delicacies fit for princes. Pisistratus drives, with Telemachus beside him, out of Pylos and across the countryside all day until nightfall, when they reach Pherae and stay with Diocles (son of Ortilochus, grandson of Alpheus). At dawn they set off again through the echoing gateway, cross the farmland, and eventually reach the end of their journey (presumably Lacedaemon) thanks to their good horses.

barriers.my_reading: Swift horses.
barriers.note: 'Fleet' was just used for ships (¶23); aloud it sounds like a noun.

barriers.my_reading: Sweets or delicacies, not meat.
barriers.note: Archaic.

barriers.quote: swaying the yoke upon their necks
barriers.my_reading: The horses, running all day, made the yoke sway on their necks; 'they' has switched from the young men to the horses.
barriers.note: Hard to picture; the subject shift is confusing.

barriers.my_reading: They arrived at Lacedaemon, Menelaus's home, though it is not named here.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The sun sets and darkness falls over the land - and the sentence, and the Book, break off there unfinished.

barriers.quote: Now when the sun had set and darkness lay over the land,
barriers.my_reading: An incomplete sentence: probably the start of the arrival at Menelaus's, continued in the next Book.
barriers.note: Ends with a comma; also unclear whether this is the same nightfall as the end of the journey in ¶36.

book_level: Athena's disguise is never stated in this Book: the narrator says 'Athena' while Telemachus calls her 'Mentor' (¶2, ¶20) and Pisistratus calls her 'sir' (¶5); only the eagle exit (¶29) confirms a goddess was present. A reader relying on this Book is unsure who 'Mentor' is and why a goddess prays to Poseidon; listeners may hear 'mentor' as the ordinary noun.

Sacrifice and feast ritual recurs in unexplained terms: 'inner meats' vs 'outer meats' (¶0, ¶4, ¶7, ¶34, ¶35), 'drink offering(s)' (¶5, ¶25, ¶26, ¶30) whose physical action (pouring wine out) is never shown, burning thigh bones, 'tongues of the victims', 'mixing-bowls', barley meal, 'a lock', 'five-pronged spits', and women who 'screamed with delight'. The gist is clear; the actions cannot be pictured.

Names for the Greeks and their places are unstable: 'Achaeans' and 'Argives' both seem to mean the whole army; 'Argos' is Diomed's home (¶14) and then Agamemnon's realm ('Achaean Argos', 'the heart of Argos', 'the people of Argos') alongside 'Mycenae'. Epithets stand in for names without being linked: 'son of Tydeus' = Diomed, 'sons of Atreus' = Agamemnon and Menelaus, 'daughter of Zeus'/'Trito-born' = Athena, 'horseman of Gerene' = Nestor.

Nestor's two long narrative paragraphs (¶14, ¶23) are very long on a phone and packed with route geography (Tenedos, Lesbos, Chios, Psyra, Mimas, Euboea, Geraestus, Sunium, Malea, Gortyn, Phaestus) that cannot be pictured without a map. ¶23 also blurs which part of Menelaus's fleet he was with and mentions Clytemnestra's funeral without saying how she died.

Much of the phrasing reads as Victorian rather than modern English: 'Presently', 'By and by', 'much of an age with myself', 'give you the precedence', 'tell me truly all', 'Who knows but that', 'made an excellent dinner', 'were for going', 'caught them up', 'look me out a heifer', 'keep open house', 'substance', 'sweetmeats', 'several errands', 'false Aegisthus', 'wooers', 'pages', 'ewer', 'stockman', 'fleet horses'.

'Heaven' (and once a singular 'God', ¶5) is used constantly for the Greek gods ('the hand of heaven', 'heaven will prompt you', 'Heaven has a long arm', 'heaven had decreed her destruction'); this gives a Christian flavour and blurs whether a particular god, the gods in general, or fate is meant.

The Book leans on earlier Books: it opens 'But ... they reached Pylos' with 'they' unidentified (and 'they' is then reused for the Pylians); the suitors (¶16) are explained only in ¶17; family links (Neleus = Nestor's father, Menelaus = Agamemnon's brother, Clytemnestra = Agamemnon's wife) arrive late or only by inference, which produces the 'Aegisthus and his wife' misreading in ¶19.

Some speeches' reasoning is hard to follow - Athena in ¶19 (the gods can save a man / not even the gods can save him), Nestor's counterfactual in ¶21, Telemachus's 'even if the gods willed it' in ¶18 - and several lines repeat word for word (¶1/¶24 'Ask him to speak the truth...', the 'rosy-fingered' dawn, 'lashed the horses on and they flew forward readily enough'), which can look like copy errors. The Book ends mid-sentence (¶37 ends with a comma).
